claim: The circadian clock enables organisms to synchronize biochemical and physiological processes over a 24 hr period.
source: The circadian clock enables organisms to synchronize biochemical and physiological processes over a 24 hr period.
evidence: This is a general statement about circadian clock function that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Natural changes in lighting conditions, as well as artificial disruptions like jet lag or shift work, can advance or delay the clock phase to align physiology with the environment.
source: Natural changes in lighting conditions, as well as artificial disruptions like jet lag or shift work, can advance or delay the clock phase to align physiology with the environment.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about how environmental light affects circadian rhythms.

claim: Within the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, circadian timekeeping and resetting rely on both membrane depolarization and intracellular second-messenger signaling.
source: Within the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, circadian timekeeping and resetting rely on both membrane depolarization and intracellular second-messenger signaling.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the mechanisms of circadian clock regulation in the SCN.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) facilitate calcium influx in both processes, activating intracellular signaling pathways that trigger Period (Per) gene expression.
source: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) facilitate calcium influx in both processes, activating intracellular signaling pathways that trigger Period (Per) gene expression.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the role of VGCCs in circadian signaling.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5) activity is modulated by light.
source: Our study in mice demonstrates that cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5) activity is modulated by light and regulates phase shifts of the circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in Cdk5 activity in response to light pulses, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cdk5 regulates phase shifts of the circadian clock.
source: Our study in mice demonstrates that cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5) activity is modulated by light and regulates phase shifts of the circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing that Cdk5 knockdown affects phase delays, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Knocking down Cdk5 in the SCN of mice affects phase delays but not phase advances.
source: We observed that knocking down Cdk5 in the SCN of mice affects phase delays but not phase advances.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1, where phase delays at ZT14/CT14 were impaired but phase advances at ZT22/CT22 were normal.

claim: Cdk5 knockdown is linked to uncontrolled calcium influx into SCN neurons.
source: This is linked to uncontrolled calcium influx into SCN neurons and an unregulated protein kinase A (PKA)-calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CaMK)-cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data in Figure 4 and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3 showing altered calcium signaling and pathway activation.

claim: Cdk5 knockdown leads to an unregulated PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway.
source: This is linked to uncontrolled calcium influx into SCN neurons and an unregulated protein kinase A (PKA)-calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CaMK)-cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figures 3 and 5 showing constitutive activation of PKA, CaMKII, CaMKIV, and CREB in the absence of light stimulation.

claim: Per1 is not induced by light in the SCN of Cdk5 knock-down mice.
source: Consequently, genes such as Per1 are not induced by light in the SCN of Cdk5 knock-down mice.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 6a, demonstrating abolished Per1 induction in shCdk5 mice.

claim: Cdk5 is a crucial light-modulated kinase that influences rapid clock phase adaptation.
source: Our experiments identified Cdk5 as a crucial light-modulated kinase that influences rapid clock phase adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined behavioral, molecular, and imaging data presented throughout the manuscript showing Cdk5's role in light-induced phase shifts.

claim: Misalignment of the internal body clock with the external light-dark cycle, caused by shift work or jet lag, leads to inefficient regulation of body functions.
source: Misalignment of the internal body clock with the external light-dark (LD) cycle, caused by shift work or jet lag, leads to inefficient regulation of body functions.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the consequences of circadian misalignment.

claim: Circadian misalignment can result in obesity, cancer, addictive behaviors, cardiovascular disease, and neurological disorders.
source: Consequently, circadian misalignment can result in obesity, cancer, addictive behaviors, cardiovascular disease, and neurological disorders (Roenneberg and Merrow, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The master circadian clock in mammals is located in the ventral part of the hypothalamus, just above the optic chiasm, in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN).
source: In mammals, the master circadian clock is located in the ventral part of the hypothalamus, just above the optic chiasm, in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN).
evidence: This represents established anatomical knowledge about the location of the master circadian clock.

claim: The SCN coordinates daily cycles of physiology and behavior.
source: These nuclei coordinate daily cycles of physiology and behavior (Hastings et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Molecular daily oscillations are generated at the cellular level by a cell-autonomous transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) involving a set of clock genes.
source: Molecular daily oscillations are generated at the cellular level by a cell-autonomous transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) involving a set of clock genes (Takahashi, 2017) and post-translational modifiers such as kinases (Hirano et al., 2016; Partch, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Post-translational modifiers such as kinases are involved in molecular daily oscillations.
source: Molecular daily oscillations are generated at the cellular level by a cell-autonomous transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) involving a set of clock genes (Takahashi, 2017) and post-translational modifiers such as kinases (Hirano et al., 2016; Partch, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Circuit-level interactions among SCN cells produce a coherent daily oscillation.
source: Circuit-level interactions among SCN cells produce a coherent daily oscillation (Allen et al., 2017), which can be modulated by light signals to match the environmental LD cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Light is perceived by melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in the eye.
source: Light is perceived by melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in the eye, and the signal produced in these cells travels via the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) to the SCN (LeGates et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The light signal travels via the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) to the SCN.
source: Light is perceived by melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in the eye, and the signal produced in these cells travels via the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) to the SCN (LeGates et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The release of glutamate at the RHT terminals stimulates AMPA/NMDA receptors, leading to Ca2+ influx into the SCN.
source: The release of glutamate at the RHT terminals stimulates AMPA/NMDA receptors, leading to Ca2+ influx into the SCN (Ding et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Light alters the activity of various kinases including DARPP-32, PKA, and CaMK.
source: Additionally, the activity of various kinases is altered, including DARPP-32 (dopamine and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein of 32 kD), PKA (protein kinase A), and CaMK (Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinases).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about light-induced signaling in the SCN.

claim: The kinase cascade culminates in the phosphorylation of CREB.
source: This cascade culminates in the phosphorylation of CREB (cyclic AMP [cAMP] response element-binding protein) (Obrietan et al., 1998; Ginty et al., 1993; Gau et al., 2002; Yan et al., 2006; Wheaton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: CREB phosphorylation promotes chromatin phosphorylation.
source: This event promotes chromatin phosphorylation (Crosio et al., 2000) and acetylation (Brenna et al., 2021) via the recruitment of CRTC1 (cAMP-regulated transcriptional co-activator 1) and the histone acetyltransferase CBP (CREB-binding protein), involving the clock protein PER2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CREB phosphorylation promotes chromatin acetylation via the recruitment of CRTC1 and CBP, involving PER2.
source: This event promotes chromatin phosphorylation (Crosio et al., 2000) and acetylation (Brenna et al., 2021) via the recruitment of CRTC1 (cAMP-regulated transcriptional co-activator 1) and the histone acetyltransferase CBP (CREB-binding protein), involving the clock protein PER2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Light induces immediate-early gene and clock gene expression in the SCN.
source: Consequently, immediate-early gene and clock gene expression is induced (Rusak et al., 1990; Albrecht et al., 1997; Shigeyoshi et al., 1997), causing a phase shift of the TTFL in oscillating cells of the SCN (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Light-induced gene expression causes a phase shift of the TTFL in oscillating cells of the SCN.
source: Consequently, immediate-early gene and clock gene expression is induced (Rusak et al., 1990; Albrecht et al., 1997; Shigeyoshi et al., 1997), causing a phase shift of the TTFL in oscillating cells of the SCN (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phase shifts manifest at the behavioral level as a change of locomotor activity onset the day after the light pulse.
source: This manifests at the behavioral level as a change of locomotor activity onset (phase shift) the day after the light pulse.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about how molecular phase shifts translate to behavioral changes.

claim: The direction of the phase shift depends on the clock's temporal state.
source: The direction of the phase shift depends on the clock's temporal state.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about circadian phase response curves.

claim: Light perceived in the early night promotes phase delays.
source: Light perceived in the early night promotes phase delays, while a light pulse late at night promotes phase advances.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about circadian phase response curves.

claim: A light pulse late at night promotes phase advances.
source: Light perceived in the early night promotes phase delays, while a light pulse late at night promotes phase advances.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about circadian phase response curves.

claim: Light in the middle of the day does not alter the clock phase.
source: Light in the middle of the day does not alter the clock phase (Daan and Pittendrigh, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Per1 and Per2 genes are important for resetting of the circadian clock in mice.
source: For this so-called resetting of the circadian clock, the Per1 and Per2 genes appear to be important in mice.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from previous studies on Per gene function.

claim: Per1 is essential for phase advances.
source: While Per1 is essential for phase advances, Per2 function is necessary for phase delays (Albrecht et al., 2001; Spoelstra et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Per2 function is necessary for phase delays.
source: While Per1 is essential for phase advances, Per2 function is necessary for phase delays (Albrecht et al., 2001; Spoelstra et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) are classified into high voltage-activated channels (including L-type) and low voltage-activated subtypes (T-type channels).
source: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) are classified into high voltage-activated channels, which include L-type, and low voltage-activated subtypes, also known as T-type channels (Catterall, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: T-type VGCCs are involved in phase delays.
source: T-type VGCCs are involved in phase delays, whereas L-type VGCCs are related to phase advances (Kim et al., 2005; Schmutz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: L-type VGCCs are related to phase advances.
source: T-type VGCCs are involved in phase delays, whereas L-type VGCCs are related to phase advances (Kim et al., 2005; Schmutz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3 belong to the T-type channel family.
source: CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3 belong to the T-type channel family, which is critically important for neuronal excitability (Perez-Reyes, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: T-type channels are critically important for neuronal excitability.
source: CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3 belong to the T-type channel family, which is critically important for neuronal excitability (Perez-Reyes, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The activity of T-type channels is regulated by PKA, PKC, and Cdk5.
source: The activity of these T-type channels is regulated by various kinases, including PKA (Kim et al., 2006), PKC (Chemin et al., 2007), and Cdk5 (cyclin-dependent kinase 5) (Calderón-Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 is a proline-directed serine/threonine kinase.
source: Cdk5 is a proline-directed serine/threonine kinase that forms a complex with its neural activators p35 or p39 (Tang et al., 1995; Tsai et al., 1994) and cyclin I (Brinkkoetter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 forms a complex with its neural activators p35 or p39 and cyclin I.
source: Cdk5 is a proline-directed serine/threonine kinase that forms a complex with its neural activators p35 or p39 (Tang et al., 1995; Tsai et al., 1994) and cyclin I (Brinkkoetter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The complex of Cdk5 and its activators controls neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and synaptogenesis.
source: The complex of Cdk5 and its activators controls various neuronal processes such as neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and synaptogenesis (Jessberger et al., 2009; Kawauchi, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 kinase activity is low in the light phase and high in the dark phase.
source: In vivo and in vitro experiments show that Cdk5 kinase activity is low in the light phase and high in the dark phase (Brenna et al., 2019; Ripperger et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 regulates the circadian clock in the SCN via phosphorylation of PER2 at serine 394.
source: It regulates the circadian clock in the SCN via phosphorylation of PER2 at serine 394.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from previous studies by the authors.

claim: Upon phosphorylation by Cdk5, PER2 is stabilized and enters the nucleus.
source: Upon phosphorylation by Cdk5, PER2 is stabilized and enters the nucleus to participate in the regulation of the TTFL and CREB-related transcriptional events (Brenna et al., 2021; Brenna et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 regulates the T-type channel CaV3.1.
source: Since Cdk5 regulates the T-type channel CaV3.1 (Calderón-Rivera et al., 2015) and the circadian clock via PER2 phosphorylation (Brenna et al., 2019), we analyzed the potential role of Cdk5 in the light-mediated clock resetting mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Silencing Cdk5 in the SCN reduced its expression in the SCN.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Brenna et al., 2019), we found that silencing Cdk5 in the SCN reduced its expression in the SCN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) and the expression of PER2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Silencing Cdk5 in the SCN reduced the expression of PER2.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Brenna et al., 2019), we found that silencing Cdk5 in the SCN reduced its expression in the SCN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) and the expression of PER2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Under constant darkness conditions, knock-down of Cdk5 shortened the clock period in male mice.
source: Under constant darkness (DD) conditions, this knock-down of Cdk5 shortened the clock period in male mice, as assessed by wheel-running activity (Figure 1a and b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1a, b, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The period of Cdk5 knock-down mice was not influenced by light pulses.
source: This period was not influenced by light pulses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Light at ZT14 delayed the clock phase in control animals.
source: Light at zeitgeber time (ZT) 14 (where ZT0 is lights on and ZT12 is lights off) delayed the clock phase, whereas light at ZT22 advanced it in control (scr) animals, with light at ZT10 having no effect (Figure 1a and c, Aschoff type II protocol).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1a and c.

claim: Light at ZT22 advanced the clock phase in control animals.
source: Light at zeitgeber time (ZT) 14 (where ZT0 is lights on and ZT12 is lights off) delayed the clock phase, whereas light at ZT22 advanced it in control (scr) animals, with light at ZT10 having no effect (Figure 1a and c, Aschoff type II protocol).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1a and c.

claim: Light at ZT10 had no effect on clock phase in control animals.
source: Light at zeitgeber time (ZT) 14 (where ZT0 is lights on and ZT12 is lights off) delayed the clock phase, whereas light at ZT22 advanced it in control (scr) animals, with light at ZT10 having no effect (Figure 1a and c, Aschoff type II protocol).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1a and c.

claim: Light did not elicit a phase delay at ZT14 in shCdk5 animals.
source: The animals with silenced Cdk5 in the SCN (shCdk5) behaved similarly to controls (scr), except for ZT14. Light did not elicit a phase delay at this time, suggesting that Cdk5 plays a role in the phase delay mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1a and c.

claim: Similar results for Cdk5 knockdown effects on phase shifts were obtained for female animals.
source: Similar results were obtained for female animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–g.

claim: Light at CT14 promoted a phase delay in scr control mice.
source: Light applied at CT14 promoted a phase delay in scr control mice. However, silencing of Cdk5 impaired the delay of the clock phase (Figure 1d and f), which is consistent with the observation at ZT14 (Figure 1a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d and f.

claim: Silencing of Cdk5 impaired the delay of the clock phase at CT14.
source: Light applied at CT14 promoted a phase delay in scr control mice. However, silencing of Cdk5 impaired the delay of the clock phase (Figure 1d and f), which is consistent with the observation at ZT14 (Figure 1a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d and f.

claim: Light at CT22 elicited normal phase advances in shCdk5 and scr controls.
source: Light at CT22 elicited normal phase advances in shCdk5 and scr controls (Figure 1d and f), similar to the light pulse applied at ZT22 (Figure 1a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d and f.

claim: Light increased the phosphorylation levels of PKA in the SCN at ZT14.
source: To ensure proper light induction, we measured the light-dependent phosphorylation of PKA (Figure 2a and b), CaMKII and CREB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d). We confirmed that PKA, CaMKII, and CREB phosphorylation levels increased in response to light in the SCN (Figure 2a and b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: Light increased the phosphorylation levels of CaMKII in the SCN at ZT14.
source: To ensure proper light induction, we measured the light-dependent phosphorylation of PKA (Figure 2a and b), CaMKII and CREB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d). We confirmed that PKA, CaMKII, and CREB phosphorylation levels increased in response to light in the SCN (Figure 2a and b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: Light increased the phosphorylation levels of CREB in the SCN at ZT14.
source: To ensure proper light induction, we measured the light-dependent phosphorylation of PKA (Figure 2a and b), CaMKII and CREB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d). We confirmed that PKA, CaMKII, and CREB phosphorylation levels increased in response to light in the SCN (Figure 2a and b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: Light increased the p35 protein level at ZT14.
source: Interestingly, we observed that light could also increase the p35 protein level, although the levels of Cdk5 remained unaffected (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2a and c.

claim: The levels of Cdk5 remained unaffected by light at ZT14.
source: Interestingly, we observed that light could also increase the p35 protein level, although the levels of Cdk5 remained unaffected (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2a and c.

claim: Cdk5 kinase activity decreased in response to light at ZT14.
source: Surprisingly, our results indicated that Cdk5 kinase activity decreased in response to light (Figure 2d and e), suggesting that light may affect the interaction between Cdk5 and p35.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: SCN extracts from mice that received a light pulse at ZT14 contained less p35 in a complex with Cdk5.
source: Our results revealed that SCN extracts from mice that received a light pulse at ZT14 contained less p35 in a complex with Cdk5 (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Light affects Cdk5 activity by interfering with the formation of the Cdk5/p35 complex.
source: Taken together, the results support the hypothesis that light affects Cdk5 activity by interfering with the formation of the Cdk5/p35 complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Figure 2 showing decreased Cdk5 activity and reduced Cdk5-p35 interaction after light.

claim: Deletion of a cAMP-responsive element (CRE) in the Per1 promoter blunted light-induced Per1 expression in the SCN at night.
source: Deletion of a cAMP-responsive element (CRE) in the Per1 promoter blunted light-induced Per1 expression in the SCN at night (Ikegami et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nocturnal light induces phosphorylation of CREB.
source: Because nocturnal light induces phosphorylation of CREB and phosphorylated CREB (p-CREB) can bind to CREs (Naruse et al., 2004; Travnickova-Bendova et al., 2002; Tischkau et al., 2003), we investigated whether Cdk5 participates in the pathway evoking the CREB phosphorylation at serine-133 (pSer-133), a site known to be involved in phase delays, and Per1 induction (Gau et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylated CREB can bind to CREs.
source: Because nocturnal light induces phosphorylation of CREB and phosphorylated CREB (p-CREB) can bind to CREs (Naruse et al., 2004; Travnickova-Bendova et al., 2002; Tischkau et al., 2003), we investigated whether Cdk5 participates in the pathway evoking the CREB phosphorylation at serine-133 (pSer-133), a site known to be involved in phase delays, and Per1 induction (Gau et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CREB phosphorylation at serine-133 is involved in phase delays and Per1 induction.
source: Because nocturnal light induces phosphorylation of CREB and phosphorylated CREB (p-CREB) can bind to CREs (Naruse et al., 2004; Travnickova-Bendova et al., 2002; Tischkau et al., 2003), we investigated whether Cdk5 participates in the pathway evoking the CREB phosphorylation at serine-133 (pSer-133), a site known to be involved in phase delays, and Per1 induction (Gau et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: p-CREB-S133 was detected in nuclei of SCN neurons after light was delivered at ZT14 in control animals.
source: In the SCN of control animals (scr), we observed p-CREB-S133 in nuclei of neurons after the light was delivered at ZT14 but not in controls (Figure 3a, arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: p-CREB-S133 was already detected in nuclei before the light pulse in shCdk5 animals.
source: In contrast, p-CREB-S133 was already detected in nuclei before the light pulse in shCdk5 animals (Figure 3a, arrowheads), indicating that Cdk5 plays a role in gating the phosphorylation of CREB.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Cdk5 plays a role in gating the phosphorylation of CREB.
source: In contrast, p-CREB-S133 was already detected in nuclei before the light pulse in shCdk5 animals (Figure 3a, arrowheads), indicating that Cdk5 plays a role in gating the phosphorylation of CREB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CREB is phosphorylated in the absence of light when Cdk5 is knocked down.

claim: CaMKII was phosphorylated after the light pulse at ZT14 in control animals.
source: Similarly, CaMKII and CaMKIV were shown to be phosphorylated and, therefore, activated only after the light pulse in control animals (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: CaMKIV was phosphorylated after the light pulse at ZT14 in control animals.
source: Similarly, CaMKII and CaMKIV were shown to be phosphorylated and, therefore, activated only after the light pulse in control animals (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: CaMKII and CaMKIV were highly phosphorylated in a light-independent manner in the SCN of shCdk5 animals.
source: Conversely, these kinases were highly phosphorylated in a light-independent manner in the SCN of shCdk5 animals (Figure 3b and d), indicating that Cdk5 had a suppressive function on the phosphorylation of CaMKII and CaMKIV.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3b and d.

claim: Cdk5 has a suppressive function on the phosphorylation of CaMKII and CaMKIV.
source: Conversely, these kinases were highly phosphorylated in a light-independent manner in the SCN of shCdk5 animals (Figure 3b and d), indicating that Cdk5 had a suppressive function on the phosphorylation of CaMKII and CaMKIV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these kinases are constitutively phosphorylated when Cdk5 is knocked down.

claim: A light stimulus can promote CaMKII alpha phosphorylation which leads to perinuclear localization of CAM in SCN cells.
source: CaMKII alpha was phosphorylated after a light pulse at ZT14, which led to perinuclear localization of CAM in control mice, while this localization pattern was already observed in shCdk5 animals independently of the light stimulus (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Perinuclear localization of CAM was already observed in shCdk5 animals independently of the light stimulus.
source: CaMKII alpha was phosphorylated after a light pulse at ZT14, which led to perinuclear localization of CAM in control mice, while this localization pattern was already observed in shCdk5 animals independently of the light stimulus (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The presence of Cdk5 suppressed the localization of Cav3.1 to the cell membrane in the absence of light.
source: Again, the presence of Cdk5 suppressed the localization of this channel to the cell membrane in the absence of light, with light allowing localization to the cell membrane (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Light allowed localization of Cav3.1 to the cell membrane.
source: Again, the presence of Cdk5 suppressed the localization of this channel to the cell membrane in the absence of light, with light allowing localization to the cell membrane (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Cdk5 plays an important role in channel translocation.
source: This observation is reminiscent of investigations described previously in which Cdk5 appeared to play an important role in channel translocation (Oberegelsbacher et al., 2011; Katz et al., 2017) as well as in receptor translocation (Liu et al., 2019; Jeong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 plays an important role in receptor translocation.
source: This observation is reminiscent of investigations described previously in which Cdk5 appeared to play an important role in channel translocation (Oberegelsbacher et al., 2011; Katz et al., 2017) as well as in receptor translocation (Liu et al., 2019; Jeong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Circadian calcium fluxes in the cytosol of SCN neurons have been demonstrated in vitro.
source: Circadian calcium fluxes in the cytosol of SCN neurons have been demonstrated in vitro (Brancaccio et al., 2013), and they change rapidly as a response to light perceived by the retina (Irwin and Allen, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Calcium fluxes in SCN neurons change rapidly as a response to light perceived by the retina.
source: Circadian calcium fluxes in the cytosol of SCN neurons have been demonstrated in vitro (Brancaccio et al., 2013), and they change rapidly as a response to light perceived by the retina (Irwin and Allen, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Calcium fluxes in the SCN of control mice increased during and after a light pulse at ZT14.
source: We observed that calcium fluxes in the SCN of control mice increased during and after a light pulse, but this change was significantly dampened in shCdk5 animals (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: The calcium flux change in response to light was significantly dampened in shCdk5 animals.
source: We observed that calcium fluxes in the SCN of control mice increased during and after a light pulse, but this change was significantly dampened in shCdk5 animals (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: The PKA signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating phase delays in photic resetting.
source: The cAMP-activated PKA signaling pathway, which leads to phosphorylation of CREB, plays a pivotal role in regulating phase delays in photic resetting (Gillette and Mitchell, 2002; Sterniczuk et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PKA signaling pathway can be induced in vivo and in vitro.
source: Since the PKA signaling pathway can be induced in vivo (Ginty et al., 1993; Tischkau et al., 2000) and in vitro (Yagita and Okamura, 2000), we investigated whether Cdk5 could play a role in PKA-mediated CREB phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The FRET signal in control cells strongly decreased between 10 and 30 min after forskolin stimulus.
source: We observed that the FRET signal in control cells strongly decreased between 10 and 30 min after the stimulus compared to baseline (Figure 5a, blue trace, the first 5 min are ignored, because they represent the diffraction of the solvent DMSO).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The FRET signal in Cdk5 ko cells rose toward baseline after an initial decline in response to forskolin.
source: In contrast, the FRET signal in Cdk5 ko cells rose toward baseline after an initial decline in response to forskolin (Figure 5a, red trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Cdk5 is involved in the phosphorylation of CREB.
source: This indicated that Cdk5 is involved in the phosphorylation of CREB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET data showing different CREB phosphorylation dynamics in Cdk5 ko cells.

claim: Ca2+-mediated CREB transcription of target genes requires PKA activity.
source: Previous studies have described that Ca2+-mediated CREB transcription of target genes requires PKA activity (Impey et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CREB phosphorylation is modulated by Cdk5 via Ca2+ signaling.
source: Together, our results indicate that CREB phosphorylation is modulated by Cdk5 via Ca2+ signaling, as suggested in Figure 3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined FRET and calcium manipulation experiments shown in Figure 5b.

claim: PKA did not appear to directly phosphorylate CREB, as CREB did not pull down p-PKA in an immunoprecipitation experiment.
source: Interestingly, PKA did not appear to directly phosphorylate CREB, as CREB did not pull down p-PKA in an immunoprecipitation experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: p-CaMKIV interacted with CREB.
source: In contrast, p-CaMKIV did interact with CREB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c), suggesting that CREB is most likely phosphorylated by CaMKIV, which is probably indirectly regulated by PKA activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: CREB is most likely phosphorylated by CaMKIV, which is probably indirectly regulated by PKA activity.
source: In contrast, p-CaMKIV did interact with CREB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c), suggesting that CREB is most likely phosphorylated by CaMKIV, which is probably indirectly regulated by PKA activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoprecipitation data and the lack of direct PKA-CREB interaction.

claim: Cdk5 regulates PKA activity via DARPP32.
source: Previous studies have shown that Cdk5 regulates PKA activity via DARPP32 (Svenningsson et al., 2004; Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DARPP32 is highly phosphorylated at ZT14, with the light signal significantly reducing the phosphorylation levels in the cytoplasm and nuclei.
source: We observed that DARPP32 is highly phosphorylated at ZT14, with the light signal significantly reducing the phosphorylation levels in the cytoplasm and nuclei (Figure 5d, blue bars; Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Silencing of Cdk5 led to a dramatic decrease in the pThr-75 DARPP32 signal in the cytoplasm and nuclei of SCN cells at ZT14.
source: In contrast, silencing of Cdk5 led to a dramatic decrease in the pThr-75 signal in the cytoplasm and nuclei of SCN cells at ZT14, and light did not have an effect (Figure 5d, red bars, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Cdk5 phosphorylates DARPP32 and light inhibits this process.
source: These observations are consistent with the view that Cdk5 phosphorylates DARPP32 and that light inhibits this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DARPP32 phosphorylation data in control and shCdk5 conditions.

claim: PKA phosphorylation significantly increased after the light pulse in the SCN tissue obtained from control mice.
source: We observed that PKA phosphorylation significantly increased after the light pulse in the SCN tissue obtained from control (scr) mice (Figure 5e, right panel, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: In SCN from shCdk5 mice, PKA phosphorylation level was already elevated before the light pulse compared to scr control.
source: However, in SCN from shCdk5 mice, the phosphorylation level was already elevated before the light pulse compared to scr control (Figure 5e, left panels, top micrographs), and it was also sustained after the light pulse (Figure 5e, left panels, bottom micrographs, right panel, red bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Cdk5 gates PKA phosphorylation induced by the light pulse at ZT14.
source: Our results indicate that Cdk5 gates PKA phosphorylation induced by the light pulse at ZT14.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PKA phosphorylation data in control and shCdk5 conditions.

claim: Active PKA can stimulate Ca2+ influx through Cav3 T-type voltage-gated channels, including Cav3.1.
source: Many observations indicate that active PKA can stimulate the Ca2+ influx through Cav3 T-type voltage-gated channels, including Cav3.1 (Chemin et al., 2007; Harraz and Welsh, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The co-localization between Cav3.1 and phospho-PKA dramatically increased after the light pulse in the SCN tissue of control mice.
source: We observed that the co-localization between Cav3.1 and phospho-PKA dramatically increased after the light pulse in the SCN tissue of control (scr) mice (Figure 5f, scr left panels yellow color, and blue bars in the right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The co-localization level between Cav3.1 and phospho-PKA was already high in the shCdk5 SCN tissue before the light pulse.
source: Interestingly, the co-localization level of the two proteins was already high in the shCdk5 SCN tissue before the light pulse, compared to controls (Figure 5f scramble vs. shCdk5, left panel, top micrographs).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Cdk5 gates the PKA-Cav3.1 interaction in response to the light signal at ZT14 in an indirect way via DARPP32.
source: Altogether our results suggest that Cdk5 gates the PKA-Cav3.1 interaction in response to the light signal at ZT14 in an indirect way via DARPP32.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing Cdk5 regulation of DARPP32, PKA, and Cav3.1.

claim: Light perceived in the dark period induces immediate early genes and certain clock genes in the SCN.
source: Light perceived in the dark period leads not only to phase shifts but also induces immediate early genes and certain clock genes in the SCN (Rusak et al., 1990; Albrecht et al., 1997; Shigeyoshi et al., 1997; Kornhauser et al., 1990; Honma et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Light-induced gene expression involves the PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway.
source: This process involves the PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway (reviewed in Golombek and Rosenstein, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Per1 mRNA expression was induced by light, peaking at 1 hr after the stimulus.
source: In agreement with previous studies, Per1 and Dec1 mRNA expression was induced by light, peaking at 1 hr after the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Dec1 mRNA expression was induced by light, peaking at 1 hr after the stimulus.
source: In agreement with previous studies, Per1 and Dec1 mRNA expression was induced by light, peaking at 1 hr after the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Per2 mRNA expression was not affected by the light pulse at ZT14.
source: Conversely, Per2 and Dec2 mRNA expression was not affected by the light pulse at ZT14 (Figure 6a–d, blue bars) (Shigeyoshi et al., 1997; Honma et al., 2002; Olejniczak et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Dec2 mRNA expression was not affected by the light pulse at ZT14.
source: Conversely, Per2 and Dec2 mRNA expression was not affected by the light pulse at ZT14 (Figure 6a–d, blue bars) (Shigeyoshi et al., 1997; Honma et al., 2002; Olejniczak et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Knock-down of Cdk5 abolished light-driven Per1 gene induction.
source: Knock-down of Cdk5 abolished this light-driven Per1 and Dec1 gene induction (Figure 6a and c, red bars), indicating the involvement of Cdk5 in the light-driven activation process of these clock genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Knock-down of Cdk5 abolished light-driven Dec1 gene induction.
source: Knock-down of Cdk5 abolished this light-driven Per1 and Dec1 gene induction (Figure 6a and c, red bars), indicating the involvement of Cdk5 in the light-driven activation process of these clock genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Expression of Bmal1 was not light-inducible and was not affected by shCdk5.
source: As previously reported, expression of the clock gene Bmal1 was not light-inducible (Brenna et al., 2019; von Gall et al., 2003) and was not affected by shCdk5 (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6e and citations to previous literature.

claim: The knock-down of Cdk5 did not affect light-mediated induction of Fos expression.
source: Interestingly, the knock-down of Cdk5 did not affect light-mediated induction of Fos expression, which peaked at 0.5 hr after the light pulse (Figure 6g).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Egr1 was light-inducible in control but not in shCdk5 animals.
source: In contrast, Egr1, another immediate early gene involved in synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory (Li et al., 2005), was light-inducible in control but not in shCdk5 animals (Figure 6h).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: The immediate early gene Fos is regulated by a different mechanism compared to Egr1 and the clock genes Per1 and Dec1 in response to a light stimulus at ZT14.
source: This suggests that the immediate early gene Fos is regulated by a different mechanism compared to Egr1 and the clock genes Per1 and Dec1 in response to a light stimulus at ZT14.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Cdk5 knockdown on Fos versus Egr1/Per1/Dec1 induction.

claim: A light pulse did not significantly induce Vip expression in the SCN.
source: We observed that a light pulse did not significantly induce Vip expression in the SCN, nor did shCdk5 affect its general expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cdk5 does not regulate Vip expression and modulate phase shifts via VIP.
source: This suggests that Cdk5 does not regulate Vip expression and modulate phase shifts via VIP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of Cdk5 knockdown on Vip expression.

claim: Sik1 is involved in the regulation of the magnitude and duration of phase shifts by acting as a suppressor of the effects of light on the clock.
source: Salt-inducible kinase 1 (Sik1) is involved in the regulation of the magnitude and duration of phase shifts by acting as a suppressor of the effects of light on the clock (Jagannath et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sik1 was significantly induced by a light pulse in the SCN of control mice after 0.5 hr.
source: We observed that Sik1 was significantly induced by a light pulse in the SCN of control mice after 0.5 hr. However, the knock-down of Cdk5 abolished this induction (Figure 6i).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: The knock-down of Cdk5 abolished Sik1 induction by light.
source: We observed that Sik1 was significantly induced by a light pulse in the SCN of control mice after 0.5 hr. However, the knock-down of Cdk5 abolished this induction (Figure 6i).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: Cdk5 modulates Sik1 expression to regulate the magnitude of the behavioral response to light.
source: This suggests that Cdk5 modulates Sik1 expression to regulate the magnitude of the behavioral response to light.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of Sik1 in limiting phase shifts and the effect of Cdk5 on Sik1 expression.

claim: The light-inducible small G-protein Gem limits the circadian clock phase-shift magnitude by inhibiting voltage-dependent calcium channels.
source: The light-inducible small G-protein Gem limits the circadian clock phase-shift magnitude by inhibiting voltage-dependent calcium channels (Matsuo et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Gem was significantly induced by light 1 hr after light administration.
source: We observed that Gem was significantly induced by light 1 hr after light administration (Figure 6j, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: Knock-down of Cdk5 abolished light-induced Gem expression.
source: Interestingly, knock-down of Cdk5 abolished this induction (Figure 6i, red bars), but Gem levels seemed to be slightly elevated already before light administration (Figure 6i, time point 0).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: Cdk5 influences light-induced Gem expression and may also affect basal Gem expression before the light pulse.
source: This indicates that Cdk5 influences light-induced Gem expression and may also affect basal Gem expression before the light pulse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Gem expression data in control and shCdk5 conditions.

claim: Phase shifts of the circadian clock can be studied in cell cultures using forskolin instead of light as a stimulus.
source: Phase shifts of the circadian clock can also be studied in cell cultures using forskolin instead of light as a stimulus (Yagita and Okamura, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of Per1 but not Per2 mRNA was induced in synchronized NIH 3T3 fibroblast cells after forskolin treatment.
source: In accordance with our in vivo experiments (Figure 6), expression of Per1 but not Per2 mRNA was induced in synchronized NIH 3T3 fibroblast cells after forskolin treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d and e, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: Per1 induction by forskolin was abolished in Cdk5 ko cells.
source: Comparable to the experiments in the SCN, Per1 induction was abolished in Cdk5 ko cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Fos mRNA induction was not affected in Cdk5 ko cells.
source: In contrast, Fos mRNA induction was not affected in Cdk5 ko cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f), consistent with our observations in the SCN (Figure 6g).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Cdk5 regulates light- and forskolin-mediated expression of genes critical for the regulation of phase delays of the circadian clock.
source: Collectively, our expression data provide evidence that Cdk5 regulates light- and forskolin-mediated expression of genes critical for the regulation of phase delays of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined gene expression data from in vivo and in vitro experiments.

claim: The phenotype of Cdk5 knock-down in the SCN of mice resembled the phenotypes observed in Per2 mutant and neuronal Per2 knock-out mice.
source: The phenotype of Cdk5 knock-down (shCdk5) in the SCN of mice resembled the phenotypes observed in Per2 mutant (Per2Brdm1) and neuronal Per2 knock-out (nPer2 ko) mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the behavioral phenotypes across different mouse models.

claim: Cdk5 is involved in the regulation of the circadian clock mechanism via nuclear localization of PER2.
source: Our results indicate that Cdk5 is not only involved in the regulation of the circadian clock mechanism via nuclear localization of PER2 but also plays an important role in the molecular mechanism that leads to a delay of clock phase in response to a light pulse in the early dark phase or early subjective night.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from previous studies by the authors.

claim: Cdk5 plays an important role in the molecular mechanism that leads to a delay of clock phase in response to a light pulse in the early dark phase or early subjective night.
source: Our results indicate that Cdk5 is not only involved in the regulation of the circadian clock mechanism via nuclear localization of PER2 but also plays an important role in the molecular mechanism that leads to a delay of clock phase in response to a light pulse in the early dark phase or early subjective night.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined behavioral and molecular data presented in the study.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CaMKII but not of MAPK affected light-induced phase delays in hamsters.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CaMKII but not of MAPK affected light-induced phase delays in hamsters (Yokota et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Darpp-32 ko mice show attenuated phase delays.
source: Furthermore, Darpp-32 ko mice show attenuated phase delays (Yan et al., 2006) resembling shCdk5 mice (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lack of Per1, Dec1, Sik1, Gem, Fos, or Egr1 alone does not abolish phase delays.
source: Interestingly, neither lack of Per1, Dec1(Albrecht et al., 2001; Rossner et al., 2008) nor Sik1 or Gem (Jagannath et al., 2013; Matsuo et al., 2022) alone abolish phase delays. Of note is that lack of Fos or Egr1 did not affect phase delays either (Honrado et al., 1996; Riedel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VIP is important in circadian light responses.
source: Furthermore, the neuropeptide VIP, which is important in circadian light responses (Jones et al., 2018), was not inducible by a light pulse at ZT14 in control as well as shCdk5 animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), indicating that Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling.
source: Furthermore, the neuropeptide VIP, which is important in circadian light responses (Jones et al., 2018), was not inducible by a light pulse at ZT14 in control as well as shCdk5 animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), indicating that Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of Cdk5 knockdown on VIP expression.

claim: Cdk5 not only regulates the light-sensitive PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway but ultimately also affects gene expression.
source: Overall, the present data suggest that Cdk5 not only regulates the light-sensitive PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway but ultimately also affects gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined signaling and gene expression data.

claim: Nuclear PER2 protein is necessary for transcriptional activation of light-responsive genes.
source: For the transcriptional activation of those genes, nuclear PER2 protein is necessary, which is regulated by Cdk5 (Brenna et al., 2021; Brenna et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The combination of lack of induction of many genes in the Cdk5-regulated pathway is responsible for the manifestation of rapid behavioral phase delays.
source: The combination of lack of induction of many genes in the Cdk5-regulated pathway is responsible for the manifestation of rapid behavioral phase delays.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined effects of Cdk5 on multiple genes and the behavioral phenotype.

claim: Cdk5 is active right after dark onset.
source: As reported previously, Cdk5 is active right after dark onset (Brenna et al., 2019), depicted as the active Cdk5/p35 complex (blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Active Cdk5 phosphorylates PER2, which translocates to the nucleus.
source: This has two consequences: (1) PER2 (red) is phosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus (Brenna et al., 2019), and (2) DARPP32 is phosphorylated and thus inhibits PKA activity (Bibb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylated DARPP32 inhibits PKA activity.
source: This has two consequences: (1) PER2 (red) is phosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus (Brenna et al., 2019), and (2) DARPP32 is phosphorylated and thus inhibits PKA activity (Bibb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Before the light pulse at ZT14, the nucleus is supplied with PER2, which appears to be necessary for light-mediated behavioral phase delays.
source: Hence, before the light pulse at ZT14, the nucleus is supplied with PER2, which appears to be necessary for light-mediated behavioral phase delays (Albrecht et al., 2001; Spoelstra et al., 2004; Chavan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Light at ZT14 evokes glutamate and PACAP release at the synapses between the RHT and the SCN.
source: This state can then be dramatically changed when light is applied at ZT14 (Figure 7b) evoking glutamate and PACAP release at the synapses between the RHT and the SCN.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about neurotransmitter release in response to light.

claim: Light at ZT14 abolishes the interaction between p35 and Cdk5, thereby inactivating Cdk5.
source: Interaction between p35 and Cdk5 is abolished (Figure 2) thereby inactivating Cdk5 and stopping phosphorylation of PER2 and DARPP32.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PKA phosphorylates Cav3.1.
source: At the same time, PKA becomes phosphorylated due to PACAP and cAMP signaling, leading to activation of Cav3.1 by PKA (Figure 5f; Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phospho-CREB builds up a complex with CRTC1/CBP and PER2 to activate gene expression.
source: Phospho-CREB builds up a complex with CRTC1/CBP and PER2 (Brenna et al., 2021) to activate gene expression of the Per1, Dec1, Sik1, and Gem genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The amount of PER2 protein in the nucleus may determine at least in part the magnitude of the phase delay.
source: In the activation complex the amount of PER2 present in the nucleus may at least in part affect the magnitude of the phase delay, which is depending on the time the light pulse is given.
evidence: This is speculation based on the role of PER2 in the transcriptional complex and the timing-dependent effects of light.

claim: Cdk5 activity gates both the pre-light condition and the post-light condition.
source: In conclusion, Cdk5 activity is gating both processes, the pre-light condition and the post-light condition, leading to a concerted activation of a set of light-responsive genes that impinge on behavioral phase delays in response to nocturnal light exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing Cdk5's role in regulating both PER2 nuclear localization and the light signaling pathway.
